paragraphs.text: When the first practical photographic processes were announced in 1839, few people thought of them as a new form of art. The early photograph was admired for its accuracy, not its beauty: it recorded every brick of a building and every hair of a sitter’s head with a precision that no painter could match, and it did so, as its inventors liked to point out, without the intervention of a human hand. That very quality made it suspect in the eyes of artists and critics. If a machine produced the image, they asked, where were the imagination, the selection and the skill that distinguished art from mere copying? Some of them refused to admit photographs to art exhibitions at all.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Photographers answered in several ways. Some argued that the photographer’s choices of subject, viewpoint, lighting and moment were acts of judgement no less artistic than a painter’s, and that two photographers standing in the same place would never produce the same picture. Others tried to make photographs look like paintings, borrowing their subjects as well as their effects. In the second half of the nineteenth century, a number of photographers combined several negatives into a single print to create elaborate scenes with many figures, and at the end of the century a movement known as pictorialism used soft focus, textured papers and hand-worked printing processes to give photographs the atmosphere of charcoal drawings or watercolours.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The painters themselves were deeply affected. Some welcomed photography as a tool and worked from photographs rather than from live models, which saved time and allowed them to study poses that no model could hold for long. Others felt that photography had taken over one of painting’s traditional tasks, the faithful recording of appearances, and that painting must now find other purposes, and some turned away from realism altogether. Historians have linked the rise of styles that emphasised colour, brushwork and personal vision, rather than exact likeness, partly to this sense that accuracy was no longer the painter’s business. Portrait painters, whose trade depended on likeness, felt the competition most directly, and many of the less successful among them became photographers themselves.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Photography also changed how people saw movement. Before the camera, no one could say with certainty how a running animal placed its feet. In the 1870s, a series of experiments using a row of cameras triggered in sequence captured a galloping horse at intervals of a fraction of a second, and showed that at one point in its stride all four of its hooves left the ground together, though not, as painters had long shown, with the legs stretched out in front and behind. The images were widely reproduced, and some painters altered the way they depicted horses as a result, although others complained that the photographs, however accurate, looked stiff and unnatural. The eye, they argued, does not see the world in frozen fractions of a second, and a painting should show movement as it is felt rather than as it is measured.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: By the early twentieth century, a new generation of photographers rejected the soft effects of pictorialism, finding the hand-worked prints of their predecessors sentimental and dishonest. They argued that photography should stop imitating painting and make the most of what only a camera could do: record sharp detail, unusual angles and fleeting moments. Their work, printed on smooth paper with a full range of tones, was exhibited in galleries and published in journals devoted to photography as an independent art. The argument over whether photographs belonged in museums was largely settled in their favour, and several major museums established photography departments in the decades that followed. Their prints could be sharp enough to show the grain of wood or the texture of skin.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Yet photography’s status as art has always sat uneasily beside its everyday uses. The same technology that produced gallery prints also produced passport pictures, advertising, scientific records and family snapshots, and the invention of cheap, easy cameras at the end of the nineteenth century turned millions of people into photographers. Snapshots were rarely composed with care, and most were never meant to be seen by strangers. Some critics have argued that this ubiquity makes it impossible to separate the art photograph from the ordinary one except by its context: an image becomes art when it hangs in a gallery, not because of anything in the image itself. Others reply that the best photographers have always been recognisable by a consistent way of seeing, whatever the subject in front of the lens.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The arrival of digital photography and the smartphone has intensified the question. Billions of photographs are now taken every day, and software can adjust, combine and even generate images that were never exposed in any camera, and many are seen once and never again. The early argument about whether a machine-made picture could be art has returned in a new form, now directed at images produced by software rather than by a lens. The history of photography suggests that such arguments are rarely settled by theory. They are settled, slowly, by what artists choose to do with the new tool and by what audiences come to value. Photography itself is the clearest example.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: The coffee house and its public

paragraphs.text: When coffee houses began to open in the cities of the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century, and in western Europe a century later, they offered something new: a public place where people could meet, sit for hours and talk, for the price of a single drink, without the drunkenness associated with taverns. Their popularity was immediate. Customers came as much for the company as for the coffee, which was often said to taste terrible. By the end of the seventeenth century, London was said to have hundreds of coffee houses, and similar establishments had spread through the commercial cities of Europe. Contemporaries were fascinated and alarmed in roughly equal measure by what went on inside them, and a lively literature of pamphlets praised and attacked the new drink and the places that served it. Some towns attempted to regulate them almost at once.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: What went on, above all, was conversation. Coffee houses were open to any man who could pay, and customers of very different social standing sat at the same tables, a mixing of ranks that some observers found exhilarating and others found disturbing. Women were generally excluded as customers, although a number of coffee houses were run by women. Newspapers, pamphlets and letters were available for customers to read, and news was discussed, argued over and passed on. Governments suspected that the coffee houses spread rumour and criticism, and several rulers tried to close them; in London, a royal order of 1675 banning them was withdrawn within days in the face of protests. The episode showed how quickly the coffee house had become part of ordinary city life.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Many coffee houses became associated with particular trades or interests. Merchants in shipping gathered in one, booksellers in another, scientists and scholars in a third, and customers visited a coffee house much as later generations would use an office or a club, to find the people and information they needed. Letters could be addressed to a customer at his usual coffee house, and some houses kept books in which notices and prices were recorded, and advertisements for goods for sale were pinned to the walls. The coffee house was, in effect, a network of information centres in an age before telephones, and a newcomer to a city could learn a great deal simply by finding the right room and listening. Many customers visited several different houses in a single day.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Several important institutions grew directly out of this arrangement. A coffee house near the London docks became the meeting place of merchants and ship owners seeking to insure their vessels, and its proprietor began publishing a list of ship movements and other shipping news to attract customers; the insurance market that developed there still carries his name. Stock traders, who were not welcome in the formal exchange, did business in nearby coffee houses, and the lists of prices they compiled were the ancestors of modern financial reports. Auctions of goods, ships and even whole cargoes were also held in coffee houses, often timed by the burning of a short candle.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Philosophers and historians have since given the coffee house a larger significance. One influential account presents it as the birthplace of a public sphere: a space, independent of both government and family, in which private individuals came together to debate matters of common concern and to form public opinion. Critics of this view point out that the coffee house was far less open than its admirers claimed, excluding women and the poor, and that much of the talk was gossip rather than reasoned debate. They also note that similar spaces, such as barbers’ shops, markets and taverns, had long served some of the same functions. Even so, the account remains influential, partly because no other space brought together such a range of people so regularly.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The coffee house declined in England during the eighteenth century, partly because coffee was heavily taxed and tea became the more popular drink, and partly because many of its functions moved into private clubs, offices and exchanges with membership rules. Elsewhere in Europe, the café remained central to city life, and in cities such as Vienna and Paris particular cafés became associated with writers, artists and political movements well into the twentieth century. Customers could spend a whole day over one cup, reading newspapers supplied by the house, and some writers treated a favourite café as their workplace, receiving visitors and even mail there.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The spread of chain coffee shops in recent decades has revived some of these habits in unexpected ways, and many such shops are designed to encourage customers to stay. People once again spend hours in a public place for the price of a drink, though now they are more likely to be looking at a laptop than talking to a stranger. Some sociologists describe such places as a third place, distinct from home and work, that supports informal community life. Others doubt that a room full of people wearing headphones can serve the functions that made the original coffee house so important. Whether or not the comparison holds, the idea that a city needs somewhere to sit, read and meet without an invitation has proved remarkably durable.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: Is it the runner or the shoe?

paragraphs.text: In the space of a few years, many of the records in long-distance road running have been broken, several of them by large margins. The improvements coincided with the arrival of a new kind of racing shoe, with a thick layer of highly responsive foam and a stiff plate, usually made of carbon fibre, running the length of the sole. Laboratory tests found that the best of these shoes reduced the energy a runner needed to maintain a given pace by around four per cent, a gain that can amount to minutes over a marathon. The sport’s governing body has responded with rules limiting the thickness of the sole, but the argument about whether the shoes are fair has not gone away. It is a debate about fairness as much as about technology.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case against the shoes begins with comparison. Records are valued because they allow athletes of different generations to be measured against one another, and a technology that makes everyone faster undermines that comparison. Nobody doubts that the athletes themselves trained as hard as ever. The sports historian Ruth Adeyemi argues that records set in the new shoes should be marked separately. She points to swimming, where full-body suits produced a flood of records before they were banned, and where many of those records then stood for years, making later swimmers look slower than they were. Her concern is less for the athletes of today than for those of the past, whose achievements now look smaller than they really were. Several former champions have expressed similar views.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: I find the swimming comparison less convincing than it first appears. Running has always changed with its equipment: spiked shoes, synthetic tracks and lighter materials all made athletes faster, and no one proposes adjusting the records set before each of them. The physiologist Daniel Park points out that the benefit of the new shoes varies considerably between individuals, depending on their weight and running style, so that the shoes do not simply add the same advantage to everyone. Heavier runners, in some tests, gained less than lighter ones. In his view, this variation is a stronger objection than the effect on records, since it means that the choice of shoe can decide a race between athletes of equal ability. He has measured differences of several per cent between runners wearing the same model.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: That concern is sharpened by questions of access, and the rivalry between manufacturers has become part of the story of every major race. When the shoes first appeared, the most advanced versions were available only to athletes sponsored by one manufacturer, and competitors under contract to other companies had to choose between their income and their chances of winning. The economist Laura Mensah, who has studied sponsorship in athletics, notes that most professional runners depend on shoe contracts for a large part of their earnings, and that a technical advantage controlled by a single company gives that company unusual power over who can compete successfully at the top of the sport. Some runners have since moved to other sponsors, often for lower fees.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The governing body’s rules have addressed some of this. Shoes used in competition must now be available for anyone to buy for a period before they are raced, which is meant to stop companies building special shoes for a single race, and the thickness of the sole is limited. Critics argue that the limits were set generously enough to allow the shoes already in use, and that they regulate the design rather than the effect. Supporters reply that no rule could measure the effect directly, since the benefit depends on the runner, and that a simple, measurable limit is better than none at all. The debate over the exact figures is likely to continue.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: It is also worth asking what the shoes have done for ordinary runners. Versions of the technology are now sold in shops, and many recreational runners report that they allow them to train with less muscle soreness and to run faster in races. The sports scientist Tomasz Nowak cautions that some of these benefits may reflect expectation rather than mechanics, since runners who believe their shoes will help often try harder, but he accepts that the laboratory evidence for a real effect is strong. The shoes are expensive, however, and wear out faster than conventional ones, so that the advantage is not equally available to everyone even at club level. Many clubs now advise newer members to buy them only once they are training regularly.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own view is that the shoes should be accepted, but that the rules should continue to evolve. Sport has never been a contest of bodies alone; it has always involved equipment, training methods and scientific knowledge, and each generation’s records reflect the resources available to it. Altitude training and new diets have also made runners faster. What matters is that the advantage is available to all competitors on equal terms, and that the rules are clear before a race rather than decided after it. Records will go on being broken, and that is not in itself a problem. It becomes one only when the winner is decided by the contract a runner has signed rather than by the race.
paragraphs.label: G

groups.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–G, from the list below.

items.quote: many of the records in long-distance road running have been broken
items.prompt: The new shoes have improved times mainly in races run on a track.

explanation.en: Road-running records are discussed; the track is never compared → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Автор тас жолдағы жүгіру рекордтары туралы айтады; жол-жолақ пен салыстыру жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Автор говорит о рекордах в шоссейном беге; о беговой дорожке и о сравнении с ней ничего нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: no one proposes adjusting the records set before each of them
items.prompt: Earlier improvements in running equipment were not followed by changes to the records.

explanation.en: “no one proposes adjusting the records set before each of them” → YES.
explanation.kk: Шиптер, синтетикалық жолақ пен жеңіл материал да жылдамдатқан, және «no one proposes adjusting the records» → YES.
explanation.ru: Шипы, синтетические дорожки и лёгкие материалы тоже ускоряли бегунов, и «no one proposes adjusting the records» → YES.

items.quote: train with less muscle soreness and to run faster in races
items.prompt: Recreational runners who use the shoes suffer fewer injuries.

explanation.en: Runners report less muscle soreness, not fewer injuries → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Әуесқой жүгірушілер бұлшықет ауыруы азайғанын айтады; жарақат туралы ештеңе жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Бегуны-любители сообщают о меньшей боли в мышцах и более быстром беге; о травмах ничего нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: competitors under contract to other companies had to choose between their income and their chances of winning
items.prompt: Athletes contracted to other companies were eventually permitted to wear the rival shoes.

explanation.en: Athletes had to choose between income and winning; later permission is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Басқа фирма спортшылары табыс пен жеңіс мүмкіндігі арасында таңдауға мәжбүр болғаны ғана айтылған; кейін рұқсат берілгені айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано лишь, что спортсменам других фирм приходилось выбирать между доходом и шансами; разрешили ли им позже — не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: they regulate the design rather than the effect
items.prompt: The current rules measure how much a shoe improves each runner’s performance.

explanation.en: The rules regulate design, not effect, which cannot be measured directly → NO, stated explicitly.
explanation.kk: Ережелер әсерді емес, құрылымды шектейді, әсерді тура өлшеу мүмкін емес → NO. Бұл анық айтылған, NOT GIVEN емес.
explanation.ru: Правила ограничивают конструкцию, а не эффект, и эффект вообще нельзя измерить прямо → NO. Это сказано явно, поэтому не NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: Records will go on being broken, and that is not in itself a problem.
items.prompt: The fact that records keep falling is not a problem in itself.

explanation.en: “Records will go on being broken, and that is not in itself a problem” → YES.
explanation.kk: «Records will go on being broken, and that is not in itself a problem» → YES.
explanation.ru: «Records will go on being broken, and that is not in itself a problem» → YES.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: whose achievements now look smaller than they really were
items.prompt: Athletes of earlier generations now appear less impressive than they were.

explanation.en: Adeyemi: past athletes’ achievements now look smaller → A.
explanation.kk: Adeyemi: бұрынғы спортшылардың жетістігі қазір кішірек көрінеді → A.
explanation.ru: Adeyemi: достижения прежних спортсменов теперь кажутся меньше, чем были → A.

items.quote: the benefit of the new shoes varies considerably between individuals
items.prompt: The shoes help some runners much more than others.

explanation.en: Park: the benefit varies with weight and running style → B.
explanation.kk: Park: пайда жүгірушінің салмағы мен техникасына байланысты → B.
explanation.ru: Park: выгода сильно зависит от веса и техники бегуна → B.

items.quote: gives that company unusual power over who can compete successfully at the top of the sport
items.prompt: A single manufacturer’s control of a technology can shape who succeeds in the sport.

explanation.en: Mensah: one company controlling the advantage gains power over who succeeds → C.
explanation.kk: Mensah: бір компания бақылайтын артықшылық оған кімнің жеңетініне билік береді → C.
explanation.ru: Mensah: преимущество под контролем одной компании даёт ей власть над тем, кто побеждает → C. Автор тоже пишет о контрактах, но это не утверждение Mensah о власти компании.

items.quote: some of these benefits may reflect expectation rather than mechanics
items.prompt: Believing in one’s equipment may itself improve results.

explanation.en: Nowak: some benefit reflects expectation rather than mechanics → D.
explanation.kk: Nowak: пайданың бір бөлігі механикадан емес, күтуден → D.
explanation.ru: Nowak: часть пользы — от ожиданий, а не от механики → D.

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D.

items.quote: reduced the energy a runner needed to maintain a given pace by around four per cent
items.prompt: What did laboratory tests show about the best new shoes?

options.text: They made runners about four minutes faster over any distance.
They cut the energy needed at a set pace by roughly four per cent.
They were four times more durable than older shoes.
They improved performance only in the final four kilometres.

explanation.en: “reduced the energy… by around four per cent” → B. A confuses the percentage with minutes.
explanation.kk: «reduced the energy… by around four per cent» → B. A пайыз бен минутты шатастырады, бұл жаңылыстыратын сан.
explanation.ru: «reduced the energy… by around four per cent» → B. A путает проценты с минутами: минуты — итог для марафона, а не для любой дистанции.

items.quote: Running has always changed with its equipment
items.prompt: Why does the writer find the swimming comparison unconvincing?

options.text: Swimming records were never affected by equipment.
Full-body suits were never actually banned.
Running has always become faster as its equipment changed.
Runners are less dependent on sponsors than swimmers.

explanation.en: “Running has always changed with its equipment” → C. B contradicts paragraph B.
explanation.kk: «Running has always changed with its equipment» → C. B B абзацына қайшы: костюмдерге тыйым салынған.
explanation.ru: «Running has always changed with its equipment» → C. B противоречит абзацу B: костюмы запретили.

items.quote: the limits were set generously enough to allow the shoes already in use
items.prompt: What do critics say about the governing body’s limits?

options.text: They were designed so that existing shoes would still be allowed.
They are too strict for recreational runners.
They measure the effect of each shoe too precisely.
They were introduced only after a major race.

explanation.en: “set generously enough to allow the shoes already in use” → A. C is the opposite.
explanation.kk: «set generously enough to allow the shoes already in use» → A. C керісінше: ереже әсерді емес, құрылымды реттейді.
explanation.ru: «set generously enough to allow the shoes already in use» → A. C — наоборот: правила регулируют конструкцию, а не эффект.

items.quote: It becomes one only when the winner is decided by the contract a runner has signed rather than by the race.
items.prompt: What does the writer see as the real danger?

options.text: That records will continue to be broken
That ordinary runners will stop buying the shoes
That rules will change too often
That sponsorship deals, not racing, will decide who wins

keywords: the contract a runner has signed

explanation.en: The danger is when the contract decides the winner → D. A is explicitly not a problem.
explanation.kk: Мәселе — жеңімпазды жарыс емес, келісімшарт анықтаса → D. A-ны автор мәселе емес дейді.
explanation.ru: Проблема — когда победителя определяет контракт, а не забег → D. A автор прямо называет не проблемой.
